Next, examine how R describes an object’s underlying storage and how its class affects the way R prints and works with it.

title: Chapter 3: Vectors
text:
Vector Types and Classes
In this section you will learn how class affects how R interprets an object and decides how it should behave.

Class and Behavior
Recall from Chapter 2 that an atomic vector contains elements of one underlying type. R can describe an object at different levels. typeof() reports its specific internal storage type, mode() reports a broader storage category, and class() reports how R interprets the object and selects methods for it. Some objects, such as dates and factors, have a class that adds meaning to their underlying storage.
For example, an object created with as.Date() has class "Date", underlying type "double", and mode "numeric". The "Date" class tells R to print and work with the object as a date.
🎯 Store any date in a variable named start_date using as.Date(). Then use mode(), typeof(), and class() to compare the underlying storage with the way R treats the object.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
start_date <- as.Date("2026-08-24")
print(start_date)


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
mode(start_date)
typeof(start_date)
class(start_date)

🗣 Modeled Comment: mode(start_date) returns "numeric", typeof(start_date) returns "double", and class(start_date) returns "Date". The class tells R to print and work with the object as a date.
Why does this matter? R uses the "Date" class to apply date-specific behavior even though the object is stored underneath as a double.
🎯 What date was it one week after start_date?

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
start_date + 7

🗣 Modeled Comment: R treats 7 as seven days and returns the date one week after start_date.


Types, Modes, and Classes
Every object has an underlying type. typeof() reports the specific internal storage type. mode() reports a broader storage category. For example, integer and double vectors both have mode "numeric".
class() reports how R should interpret an object. For an ordinary double vector, typeof() returns "double" while class() returns "numeric". For an object with a special class, such as a date or factor, the class adds meaning and affects how functions print and work with it.
Common Atomic Vector Types:

double: numbers such as 1 and 3.14
integer: whole numbers explicitly marked with L, such as 1L and 2L
character: text strings such as "Hello World" and "R is fun"
logical: TRUE, FALSE, or NA
complex: complex numbers such as 1 + 2i

Classes Used in This Chapter:

Date: a class for dates, usually built on double storage, such as as.Date("2026-01-01")
factor: a class for categorical data, built on integer codes and a set of category labels called levels



Character Strings
A character string is a sequence of characters enclosed in quotes. Character strings are used to represent text data in R.
The paste() function in R is used to concatenate (combine) strings together. It takes multiple string arguments and combines them into a single string, with an optional separator between them.

✍️ Transparency Memo Example



R Notebook using paste() to combine “yellow” and “banana” into “yellow banana,” then class(sentence) returning “character,” followed by a memo noting confusion about what “character” means.



🧐 Notice: The student used 🪞 Reflect to record an unexpected result and a specific question about the word "character". A useful next step would be to review the chapter, ask a peer or instructor, or consult another resource allowed for the work. If a resource helps, use 👀 Cite to identify it and explain what it contributed.


paste() works across vectors too, combining elements element-wise.
🎯 Create two character vectors named first_names and last_names, then use the paste() function to combine them into a new vector named full_names.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
first_names <- c("Demi", "Snoop", "Ed")
last_names <- c("Moore", "Dogg", "Sheeran")
full_names <- paste(first_names, last_names)


# ✅ Check the full_names vector
print(full_names)

🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows the full names created by combining the first and last names element-wise.
🌳 If you don’t want spaces, try paste0(first_names, last_names).


Factor Vectors (Categorical Data)
A factor is R’s way of storing categorical data. Factors store values that come from a fixed set of categories, such as “freshman,” “sophomore,” “junior,” and “senior.” Factors are common in data analysis because they help R treat categories correctly in tables, summaries, and models.
A factor often prints labels that look like character values, but its internal storage and class are different. R stores a standard factor using integer codes and uses its levels to connect those codes with category labels.

Creating Factors
The function factor() creates a factor from a vector. Character input is common because the vector values become category labels.
📜 The SYNTAX (basic):
factor(x)
Here, x is the vector you want to convert into a factor.
🎯 Create a factor vector named grades that contains the following letter grades: “A”, “B”, “C”, “A”, “B”, “A” using the factor() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
grades <- c("A", "B", "C", "A", "B", "A")
grades <- factor(grades)

🗣 Modeled Comment: The object grades is overwritten as a factor using the factor() function because the same name is used in the assignment process grades <-.

# ✅ Check the grades factor
mode(grades)
typeof(grades)
class(grades)
print(grades)

[1] "numeric"
[1] "integer"
[1] "factor"
[1] A B C A B A
Levels: A B C
🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows that the grades object has class "factor". Underneath, R stores the factor using integer codes, even though it prints the category labels.


Levels and Ordering
The printed output above displays the levels of the factor. Levels are the possible category labels a factor can contain. A factor can retain a level even when no current element uses it. Unless you specify levels, R generally creates levels from the observed values and orders character labels alphabetically.
Even though factors print category labels, R stores a standard factor underneath as integer codes. typeof() reports the internal type as "integer", mode() reports the broader mode as "numeric", and class() reports "factor". You can control the possible categories and their order by supplying the levels argument when creating the factor.
🎯 Create a factor vector named sizes with levels ordered as "Small", "Medium", and "Large" using the factor() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
sizes <- c("Medium", "Large", "Small", "Medium", "Large")
sizes <- factor(sizes, levels = c("Small", "Medium", "Large"))


# ✅ Check the sizes factor
print(sizes)

🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows the sizes factor with levels ordered as "Small", "Medium", and "Large", as specified in the factor() function.

✍️ Transparency Memo Example



R Notebook creating a character vector of class standings, converting it to a factor, and showing levels() plus mode()/typeof() outputs; memo questions why the factor prints words but stores integer codes, with a follow-up memo summarizing the explanation (integer codes + levels labels).



🧐 Notice: This is a ✍️ transparent record because the student used ✅ Check to compare class, mode, type, and levels; used 🪞 Reflect to record the contradiction between integer storage and printed words; and used 👀 Cite to identify ChatGPT and summarize what it contributed to the final understanding.

This is a high-quality memo because it captures confusion, gathers diagnostic evidence, and then resolves the confusion with a correct explanation.

Next, examine what happens when values of different types are combined in one atomic vector.



Data Coercion
An atomic vector stores elements of one type. If you try to mix types, R will coerce (convert) them to a common type based on a hierarchy of flexibility.
🎯 What happens if you mix numbers and characters?

mixed <- c("candy", 4, "book", 92)

# ✅ Check the mixed vector
print(mixed)
class(mixed)

🗣 Modeled Comment: The values 4 and 92 print as character values because the entire vector was coerced to character.
An atomic vector stores elements of one underlying type. Mixing types triggers coercion to a common type. A common coercion order is logical → integer → double → complex → character. R moves toward a type that can represent all the elements.

Converting Between Types
You can explicitly convert between types using functions like as.numeric(), as.character(), and as.logical().
The as.numeric() function tries to convert characters to numbers. If it can’t, it returns NA (not available).
📜 The SYNTAX (basic):
as.numeric(x)
🎯 Try converting a character vector of numbers to numeric using the as.numeric() function.

as.numeric(c("1", "2", "3")) # character → numeric: text converts to numbers

🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows the numeric values 1, 2, and 3 successfully converted from character strings.
🎯 Try converting the mixed vector to numeric using the as.numeric() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
as.numeric(mixed)            # character → numeric: text converts to NA

🗣 Modeled Comment: The output shows NA for "candy" and "book" because those text values cannot be converted to numbers. The character values "4" and "92" can be converted to numeric values, so they become 4 and 92.
R also gives the warning NAs introduced by coercion because some character values could not be converted to numbers. The warning tells you to inspect the new NA values and determine which conversions failed.

title: Chapter 3: Vectors
text:
Chapter Terms
Backtick: The ` character (above the Tab key) used for code-related formatting and quoting. In Markdown, single backticks mark inline code and triple backticks create fenced code blocks; in R Markdown, backticks also mark inline R code (`r …`), including inside YAML fields like date: “`r Sys.Date()`”, which gets evaluated when you render the document. In R, backticks can also quote non-syntactic names (e.g., names with spaces) so they can be used safely in code.
Coercion: The process by which R converts values of different types to a common type when they are combined in a vector. For example, if you combine numbers and characters, R will coerce the numbers to characters.
Character String: A single piece of text in R, stored as a character value and written in quotes (for example, “My favorite color is yellow!” or “Who stole the cookie from the cookie jar?”).
Class class(): A function that reports the object’s class, which tells R how to interpret the object and which methods to use when functions are applied to it. For example, class(3.14) returns "numeric", and class(mtcars) returns "data.frame".
Code Chunks: Fenced blocks in an R Markdown or Quarto document that contain executable code, usually beginning with ```{r} and ending with three backticks. Code can be run interactively or during rendering. Depending on RStudio settings, output may appear below the chunk or in another relevant pane.
Factor Class: An R object class for categorical data, where each value is stored as an integer code that points to a category label. Factors help R handle categories correctly in tables, plots, and statistical models, even though they may print like text.
Factor Levels: The distinct category labels a factor can take (for example, "freshman", "sophomore", "junior", "senior"). Levels define the set and order of categories, and each factor value is internally stored as the index of its level.
Markdown: A lightweight plain-text formatting syntax used to write structured documents (headings, lists, links, emphasis, code) in a way that stays readable as plain text and can be rendered into formats like HTML on many platforms and tools.
NA: A special constant that marks a missing value (“Not Available”)—meaning the data point is unknown or not recorded. R also provides typed missing values like NA_integer_, NA_real_, NA_character_, and NA_complex_ to match the underlying data type.
Object Name: The variable name you assign with <- that refers to the entire object in your environment. You use the object name to print, modify, or pass the whole object to functions.
Package: An installable collection of R code—functions, documentation, and sometimes datasets—that adds new features beyond base R. Packages are commonly installed from CRAN and then loaded with library() so you can use their tools in your session.
R Markdown: A document format (.Rmd) that mixes plain-text writing (Markdown) with embedded R code chunks, so you can generate reports that combine narrative, code, and computed output. You can render an R Markdown file into finished formats like HTML, PDF, or Word.
R Notebook: An .Rmd document that combines Markdown writing with R code chunks. You can run code interactively and view results below chunks or in another relevant pane, depending on your RStudio settings. Rendering creates a finished document that combines narrative, code, and computed output.
Recycling: R’s rule for handling vector operations when vectors have different lengths. R repeats the shorter vector as needed and then performs the operation element by element. If the longer length is not an exact multiple of the shorter length, R issues a warning. If it is an exact multiple, recycling occurs silently, so you should still verify that recycling was intentional.
Research Journal: A running record of your analysis and learning process. This includes the questions you asked, code you tried, outputs you received, resources you consulted, and decisions you made. In practice, you can maintain this record in an R Script or R Notebook using notes, comments, checks, and citations.
Transparency: The practice of disclosing the methods, materials, assumptions, values, and interests that shaped the work. In an R Notebook, transparency means keeping relevant code, output, decisions, checks, and resource use visible so the process can be examined.
Vector: A fundamental R data structure. Atomic vectors store elements of one underlying type, while lists can contain elements of different types and lengths. In this chapter, vector refers primarily to atomic vectors created with functions such as c().
Vector Arithmetic: Performing mathematical operations directly on vectors. In R, operations such as +, -, *, /, and ^ are applied element by element, so c(1, 2, 3) + c(10, 20, 30) returns c(11, 22, 33).
Vectorization: Writing an operation so it works directly with a vector instead of processing one element at a time in an explicit loop. In element-wise operations, R pairs corresponding elements and returns a vector of results. Other vectorized functions may summarize or otherwise transform the complete vector.
Warning: A console message indicating that R did run the command but detected a potential problem. Execution continues and a result is produced, but the output may be incomplete, unexpected, or based on an assumption (for example, coercing types, removing missing elements, or using a function in a way that may not behave as intended).
YAML Header: The metadata section at the top of an R Markdown or Quarto document, written between --- lines, that controls document settings like the title, author, date, output format (HTML/PDF/Word), and options for rendering.

R Notebooks—Part 2
In Chapter 3, you learned how to use an R Notebook (.Rmd) as a “reproducible thinking” document: code + output + memo-style writing in one place, in order. This section is a quick setup review before you begin the Chapter 4 work.
Here’s what you can do now:

Create and save an R Notebook (File > New File > R Notebook) and store it in your course folder.
Recognize the YAML header at the top of the file and edit the title.
Insert code chunks using the Insert button, a shortcut, or typed fences, and use chunks to organize the R code in your notebook.
Run chunks using the play button, Run menu, or keyboard shortcuts and see output directly below.
Memo correctly:

Inside a code chunk: text must start with # otherwise R tries to run it.
Outside a code chunk: write normal paragraphs with no # needed.
Use the notebook to document your learning process, including your goal, checks, explanations, and resources used.


An R Notebook is only useful if a person can read and understand it. In this chapter, you will keep building clean notebook habits: preserving the YAML header, organizing your work clearly, writing readable memos, and preparing a notebook that can knit successfully to HTML.

Default Text
🎯 Please open a new R Notebook in your course folder named chapter4_notes.Rmd.
When you create a new R Notebook or R Markdown file, RStudio provides a template. It is designed to demonstrate the three core components of a notebook:

The YAML header: The block of text at the very top, enclosed between two lines of three dashes (---). This tells RStudio how to knit, or render, your document.
Markdown Text: The white background text (like “This is an R Markdown Notebook”). This shows you how to write regular prose.
Code Chunks: The gray boxes containing code (like plot(cars)). This shows you how to embed executable R code.


Clear the Default Notebook Body
To start fresh, delete all the default text in the R Notebook so you have a blank canvas to work with.

Keep the Header
Do not delete the text at the very top between the — lines. This is your metadata (Title, Author, Output format). If you delete this, your file might not run correctly.
Your header should look something like this:
---
title: "Chapter 4"
output: html_notebook
---
Keep this top section. Delete the example text and code below it.


Delete the Body
You can safely delete everything below the second --- line. Keep the YAML header at the top.

Place your cursor on the line immediately following the second ---.
Highlight everything all the way to the bottom of the document.
Press Delete or Backspace.



Save the Blank Notebook
After clearing the default text, save your blank notebook as chapter4_notes.Rmd in your course folder. This will be your working file for Chapter 4.


Type a memo

I cleared the default text because the default text is just an example and I want to start with a blank notebook to practice writing my own memos and code. I kept the YAML header because it contains important information about the document, such as the title and output format, which is necessary for the notebook to knit correctly.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Transparency
Science is not just about numbers; it is also about the values that guide how and why we do our work. Researchers, policymakers, and the general public must be able to trust scientific expertise for this work to have meaning (Resnik & Elliott, 2023). Transparency in academic work promotes that trust. Transparency means disclosing methods, materials, assumptions, values, and interests so another person can understand what you did and reproduce it (Resnik & Elliott, 2023).
Transparency is associated with these three related values:

Honesty means reporting what actually happened, including shortcuts, mistakes, unexpected results, and outside help. You record what you tried even when it did not produce the result you expected. You state what you do not know yet. You do not present outside work as your own. If you use a peer, website, AI tool, instructor, or other resource, document what you used and what you learned.
Openness means making your work inspectable so someone else can see what you used and how you got your result. Reproducibility is a key part of openness. In this course, that means sharing the data source, code, steps, and explanations needed for someone else to follow your workflow.
Accountability means taking responsibility for your work. In this course, accountability means checking your results, correcting mistakes, responding to feedback, and documenting your process clearly enough that someone else can understand your choices.

Research journals are the running records of your R analysis process. They are internal documents that help you prepare reports, return to old work, and explain your decisions.
In this course, your R Notebook works like a research journal. Add comments before or near your code explaining:

🎯 Goal: What are you trying to do?
💬 Prediction: What do you expect the code to produce?
⚡ Code/Test: What code did you use to test your idea?
✍️ Record what you tried: What did you try, including code that did not work?
✅ Verify: How did you check whether the result was correct?
🗣 Comment: What does the output mean?
🪞 Reflect: What did you learn, and how could this help you later?
👀 Resource Cited: What resource did you use, and what did you learn from it?

You do not need every memo label for every small line of code. Use memo labels when your own code does something surprising, confusing, or important to check.

Next, you will practice these transparency habits while learning how R labels vector elements and selects specific values.

Indexing Vectors
The indexing operator [ is the standard way to extract parts of a vector. The basic pattern is x[i], where x is the vector and i is the index, or indices, of the elements you want to extract. For the atomic vectors in this chapter, [ ] can select one element or many, and it returns an object of the same type as x.
An index is a value used to identify elements in an object. In R, indices are often integers for positions, character values for names, or logical values such as TRUE and FALSE.

Positional Indexing
Positional indexing uses the numeric positions of elements in the vector to retrieve specific values.
🎯 Goal Use [ ] with index positions to extract values from a vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z <- c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50) # create a vector


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z[1]       

[1] 10


🗣 This returns the first element by position.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z[3]      

[1] 30


🗣 This returns the third element by position.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z[2:4]     

[1] 20 30 40


🗣 This returns the second, third, and fourth elements by position.

🧐 Notice: z[2:4] selects positions 2 through 4. It does not search for the values 2, 3, and 4.


# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
z[-c(1, 5)] 

[1] 20 30 40


🗣 Negative indexing excludes specified positions from the returned result. z[-c(1, 5)] returns all elements except the first and last. The stored z object remains unchanged because the result was not assigned to an object.

🧐 Notice: R counts positions starting at 1, not 0. Negative positions exclude those positions from the returned result. They do not delete values from the original vector.



Character Indexing
When a vector has names, you can use those names to index into the vector. Character indexing uses the names of the elements to retrieve specific values.
There are two different naming ideas here.

Object name is the variable name nerdy_palette that you use to refer to the entire vector.
Element names are the labels assigned to each element within the vector (e.g., "Octarine", "TARDIS Blue").

Element names can be used in indexing to access specific elements of the vector. A named vector works like a small lookup table: each value has a label, and you can use the label to retrieve the matching value.
🎯 Goal: Create a named vector of color codes, then use character indexing to return the hexadecimal color code for "Octarine".

# Create nerdy_palette
nerdy_palette <- c(
  "Octarine" = "#7F00FF",
  "TARDIS Blue" = "#003B6F",
  "Rebeccapurple" = "#663399",
  "Hooloovoo" = "#4F97A3",
  "Cosmic Latte" = "#FFF8E7",
  "Vantablack" = "#000000",
  "Matrix Green" = "#03A062",
  "Source Engine Magenta" = "#FF00FF",
  "Command Red" = "#CC0000",
  "Impossible Green" = "#4D9E68"
)

# Use character indexing to return the hex code for Octarine
nerdy_palette["Octarine"]

 Octarine 
"#7F00FF" 


🗣 When you run this chunk, it should return the hexadecimal color code for "Octarine" from the nerdy_palette vector.
Character indexing requires exact matching on names. If you ask for a name that doesn’t exist, you get NA for that element.
🎯 Use character indexing to retrieve the color codes for “Octarine,” “TARDIS Blue,” and “NotAColor” from the nerdy_palette vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
nerdy_palette[c("Octarine", "TARDIS Blue", "NotAColor")]

   Octarine TARDIS Blue        <NA> 
  "#7F00FF"   "#003B6F"          NA 


🗣 The output should return the color codes for "Octarine" and "TARDIS Blue", plus NA for "NotAColor" because that name does not exist in the vector.


More Indexing by Position
🎯 Use positional indexing to return the first and third color codes from the nerdy_palette vector.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
nerdy_palette[c(1, 3)]

     Octarine Rebeccapurple 
    "#7F00FF"     "#663399" 


🗣 The output shows the hexadecimal color codes for Octarine and Rebeccapurple in the nerdy_palette vector.
We will return to indexing in later chapters when we learn about data frames.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Logical Vectors
📖 Review from Chapter 2.
Logical vectors are used for conditions and comparisons.
🎯 Create a logical vector named real that contains the values TRUE, FALSE, and NA using the c() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
real <- c(FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, NA)


# ✅ Check the real vector
print(real)

 [1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE    NA


🗣 The output prints the logical values stored in the real vector.


Comparison Operators
Logical vectors can also be created using comparison operators. These operators compare values and usually return TRUE or FALSE. A comparison involving a missing value will usually return NA because R cannot determine whether the comparison is true or false.
Comparison operators include:

> greater than
< less than
== equal to
>= greater than or equal to
<= less than or equal to
!= not equal to

🎯 Create a logical vector named logicals that contains the results of the following comparisons: 1 > 2, 3 < 5, and 4 == 4 using the c() function.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
logicals <- c(1 > 2, 3 < 5, 4 == 4) 


# ✅ Check the logicals vector
print(logicals)

[1] FALSE  TRUE  TRUE


🗣 The output shows the results of the comparisons stored in the logicals vector. There is one FALSE value and two TRUE values. The first value is FALSE because 1 is not greater than 2. The second value is TRUE because 3 is less than 5. The final value is TRUE because 4 is equal to 4.


Logical Indexing
Logical indexing uses a logical vector inside [ ]. Values paired with TRUE are kept, and values paired with FALSE are left out. An NA in the logical vector produces an NA in the result because R cannot determine whether the matching value should be kept.
🎯 Create a new vector called smaller that contains only the values in number_list that are less than or equal to 20.

# ⚡ Type this in your R Notebook
number_list <- c(10, 25, 5, 30, 15, 40)

🗣 The number_list vector contains the values 10, 25, 5, 30, 15, and 40.

# ⚡ Step 1: create the logical "mask"
mask <- number_list <= 20

# ✅ Check the mask
print(mask)

[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE


🗣 This prints a logical vector (TRUE/FALSE) the same length as number_list. Each TRUE marks a value that is less than or equal to 20.
⚠️ For predictable logical indexing, use a logical vector with the same length as the vector being filtered. If the logical vector is shorter, R may recycle it. If it is longer, the result can extend beyond the available values and include NA. A length mismatch is a reason to stop and check the mask.

# ⚡ Step 2: use the logical vector inside [ ]
smaller <- number_list[mask]
print(smaller)

[1] 10  5 15


🗣 This keeps only the values where mask is TRUE, so smaller contains 10, 5, and 15.
The key idea is that the condition number_list <= 20 creates a logical vector, and [ ] uses that logical vector as a filter.

Summary
In this chapter, you strengthened your R Notebook habits by practicing transparency in your code memos. You learned to document your goals, explain what your code produced, verify your results, and record outside resources when you used help. These habits make your work easier to understand, check, revise, and share.
You also learned how to select values from vectors. You practiced positional indexing to select elements by number, negative indexing to remove elements, and character indexing to select elements from named vectors. You saw that character indexing requires exact matching and returns NA when a requested name does not exist.
Finally, you learned how logical vectors support filtering. You created logical values with comparison operators, stored those results in a logical vector, and used logical indexing to keep only the values that met a condition.
Your main takeaway is that transparent notebooks make your coding choices inspectable, and indexing gives you control over which vector values you select or filter.

title: Chapter 4: Structures
text:
Chapter Terms
Accountability: Taking responsibility for the results you report by verifying them, responding to questions or critiques, and correcting errors when found. In practice, this means you keep a clear record (e.g., in an R Markdown/Notebook or script) that shows how you checked your work and why you made your choices.
Character Indexing: Indexing a named vector using element names (character strings) instead of numbers. Names must match exactly; a missing name returns NA.
Code Chunks: Fenced blocks in an R Markdown or Quarto document that contain executable code, usually beginning with ```{r} and ending with three backticks. Code in a chunk can run interactively or during rendering. Depending on RStudio settings, output may appear below the chunk or in another relevant pane.
Comparison Operators: Operators that compare values. Common comparison operators are ==, !=, <, >, <=, and >=. They usually return TRUE or FALSE; a comparison involving a missing value will usually return NA.
Element Names: The individual labels assigned to elements inside a named vector (for example, "Octarine" or "TARDIS Blue"). Element names let you index by label (e.g., nerdy_palette["Octarine"]) to retrieve specific values.
Honesty: Accurately reporting what you did in R—your actual steps, mistakes, revisions, and uncertainty—without presenting outside work as your own. This includes clearly attributing code, ideas, and any AI assistance, and being able to explain the code you submit.
Index: A value used inside a subsetting operator to identify which part of an object to extract or replace. In R, an index can use positions, names, or logical values; for example, x[2] uses a positional index to select the second element, while df[rows, columns] uses row and column indices to select parts of a data frame. R documentation also calls these values indices or subscripts.
Indexing Operator: The single square-bracket operator [ used to extract or replace selected parts of an object. For a vector, x[i] returns the elements identified by the positions, names, or logical values supplied in i.
Logical Indexing: Using a logical vector inside [ to select values. TRUE keeps the matching value, FALSE excludes it, and NA produces an unknown element represented by NA. A shorter logical index may be recycled, so checking that the index and source vector have the same length helps prevent unintended results.
Logical Mask: A logical vector used inside the single square bracket operator [ to filter another object. Each TRUE marks a value or row to keep, and each FALSE marks a value or row to leave out; for the cleanest results, the mask should line up element-by-element with the object being filtered. For example, number_list <= 20 creates a logical mask, and number_list[mask] uses that mask to keep only the matching values.
Logical Vector: A vector that stores Boolean elements: TRUE or FALSE (and sometimes NA for missing). Logical vectors are commonly produced by comparisons (for example, x > 0) and are heavily used for filtering and conditional code
Markdown: A lightweight plain-text formatting syntax used to write structured documents (headings, lists, links, emphasis, code) in a way that stays readable as plain text and can be rendered into formats like HTML on many platforms and tools.
NA: A special constant that marks a missing value (“Not Available”)—meaning the data point is unknown or not recorded. R also provides typed missing values like NA_integer_, NA_real_, NA_character_, and NA_complex_ to match the underlying data type.
Named Vectors: Vectors that have labels attached to their elements via the names() attribute, so you can refer to values by name instead of only by position. Named vectors are useful as simple lookup tables (for example, retrieving a hex code by a color name).
Negative Indexing: Using negative integers inside the single bracket operator [ to exclude elements (or rows/columns) by position (e.g., x[-2] drops the 2nd element; df[ , -c(8, 9)] drops columns 8 and 9). In base R, negative and positive indices can’t be mixed in the same subset (except 0)
Object Name: The variable name you assign with <- that refers to the entire object in your environment. You use the object name to print, modify, or pass the whole object to functions.
Openness: Making your analysis inspectable and reproducible by sharing the inputs and decisions that produced your results (data source, packages, code, and key assumptions). In this course, openness means you provide others with enough details so thay are able to rerun your work and get the same outputs.
Positional Indexing: Indexing a vector using numeric positions (for example, x[1] for the first element or x[c(1, 3)] for the first and third). Positions are based on the current order of the vector.
R Notebook: An .Rmd (R Markdown) document that lets you run code in chunks and see the results (output, tables, plots) immediately below each chunk. It’s designed for reproducible work because it keeps your code, results, and explanatory notes together in the same file.
Research Journal: A running record of your R analysis process. This inlcudes what question you asked, what code you tried (including failed attempts), what outputs you got, and what decisions you made along the way. In practice, it’s maintained in an R script or R Markdown/Notebook with dated notes, comments, and citations so you (or someone else) can retrace, verify, and reproduce the work.
Transparency: The practice of clearly disclosing your methods, materials, assumptions, tools, values, and sources so another person can follow your workflow, reproduce your results, and evaluate your claims. In this course, transparency supports explanatory power (you can explain what your code does and why) and originality/accountability (you produce and attribute work honestly, including documenting if and how you used AI).
YAML Header: The metadata section at the top of an R Markdown or Quarto document, written between --- lines, that controls document settings like the title, author, date, output format (HTML/PDF/Word), and options for rendering.
